QuestionText: Who is known as the Father of the Indian Nation?
Options: A) Jawaharlal Nehru
B) Mahatma Gandhi
C) Sardar Patel
D) Subhas Chandra Bose
Explanation: Mahatma Gandhi (Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, 1869-1948) is honoured as the Father of the Nation (Rashtrapitta). He led India's independence movement through non-violent civil disobedience (Satyagraha). Major movements: Non-Cooperation (1920-22), Civil Disobedience/Dandi Salt March (1930), Quit India (1942). 'Gandhi Jayanti' (October 2 — his birthday) is a national holiday; also the UN International Day of Non-Violence. Assassinated January 30, 1948 by Nathuram Godse.

QuestionText: Which article of the Indian Constitution abolishes untouchability?
Options: A) Article 14
B) Article 15
C) Article 17
D) Article 21
Explanation: Article 17: 'Untouchability is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of untouchability shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.' The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (previously Untouchability Offences Act) and the SC and ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 give legal teeth to Article 17. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar (who faced extreme caste discrimination) championed this provision as the Constitution's chief architect.

QuestionText: What is the Preamble of the Indian Constitution?
Options: A) The first amendment to the Constitution
B) An introductory statement declaring India a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic committed to Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity
C) The list of Fundamental Rights
D) The schedule of official languages
Explanation: India's Preamble: 'We, the People of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a SOVEREIGN SOCIALIST SECULAR DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC and to secure to all its citizens: JUSTICE (social, economic, political); LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship); EQUALITY (of status and opportunity); FRATERNITY (assuring dignity and unity of the Nation).' 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Preamble reflects the Constitution's spirit. Supreme Court ruled it's non-justiciable (cannot override other provisions) but guides interpretation.

QuestionText: Who was the first President of India?
Options: A) Dr. S. Radhakrishnan
B) Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
C) Dr. Rajendra Prasad
D) Jawaharlal Nehru
Explanation: Dr. Rajendra Prasad (1884-1963) was India's first President (January 26, 1950 – May 13, 1962) — the only President to serve two full terms. He presided over the Constituent Assembly when the Constitution was adopted. A lawyer and freedom fighter from Bihar who participated in Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience movements. He received the Bharat Ratna in 1962. Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the 2nd President (and former VP whose birthday September 5 is Teachers' Day). Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was Constitution's chief architect, not President.

QuestionText: The Indian Constitution came into effect on:
Options: A) August 15, 1947
B) November 26, 1949
C) January 26, 1950
D) October 2, 1948
Explanation: January 26, 1950: Indian Constitution came into force — India became a Sovereign Democratic Republic. This date was chosen because the Congress had declared 'Purna Swaraj' (Complete Independence) on January 26, 1930. November 26, 1949: Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly (Constitution Day/Samvidhan Divas). August 15, 1947: India gained independence from Britain. The Constituent Assembly (1946-1949) spent 2 years 11 months 18 days drafting the Constitution — the world's longest written constitution.

QuestionText: What are Fundamental Rights in India?
Options: A) Rights available only to Indian citizens
B) Basic rights guaranteed by the Constitution to all persons (not just citizens) that are justiciable and enforceable by courts
C) Rights that can be taken away by Parliament at any time
D) Rights applicable only during normal times, suspended during emergencies
Explanation: Fundamental Rights (Part III, Articles 12-35): guaranteed to all persons (some only to citizens): Right to Equality (Articles 14-18), Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22 — speech, assembly, movement, profession, protection against arrest), Right Against Exploitation (Articles 23-24 — no forced labour, no child labour), Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28), Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30), Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32 — Dr. Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution). Justiciable: enforceable by courts. Some can be suspended during national emergency.

QuestionText: What is the 'Dandi March' (Salt Satyagraha) of 1930?
Options: A) A protest march against British taxation on cotton
B) Mahatma Gandhi's 390 km march to Dandi to make salt from seawater, defying the British salt monopoly — starting Civil Disobedience Movement
C) A march by Indian soldiers refusing to fight in World War I
D) A rally demanding complete independence in 1930
Explanation: Dandi March (Salt March): March 12 – April 6, 1930. Gandhi led 78 followers on a 390 km march from Sabarmati Ashram (Ahmedabad) to Dandi (Gujarat coast) to make salt from seawater — defying the British salt monopoly (salt tax). Triggered the Civil Disobedience Movement — millions broke salt laws, picketed liquor shops, boycotted British goods. Gandhi arrested May 1930. The march drew international attention to India's independence struggle. Time magazine named Gandhi 'Man of the Year 1930.' This was a turning point in India's freedom struggle.

QuestionText: Which article of the Indian Constitution grants Right to Life and Personal Liberty?
Options: A) Article 14
B) Article 19
C) Article 21
D) Article 32
Explanation: Article 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' Supreme Court has interpreted Article 21 very broadly to include: right to privacy (landmark 2017 Puttaswamy judgment), right to education (before Article 21A), right to food, right to health, right to live with dignity, right to a clean environment, right to bail in certain cases. This is one of the most powerful and frequently invoked fundamental rights. Available to all persons (not just citizens), even against the state.

QuestionText: Who was Bhagat Singh?
Options: A) A revolutionary freedom fighter who was hanged by the British in 1931
B) A Mughal general who fought the British
C) The first Governor of Punjab after independence
D) A poet of the Indian independence movement
Explanation: Bhagat Singh (1907-1931): iconic revolutionary freedom fighter from Punjab. With Rajguru and Sukhdev, assassinated British police officer John Saunders (1928) to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai's death. Threw bombs in Central Legislative Assembly (1929) to 'make the deaf hear.' Hanged March 23, 1931 at age 23 — considered a martyr. Advocated socialist ideology and armed resistance against British rule — different from Gandhi's non-violence. 'Inquilab Zindabad' (Long live revolution) was his slogan. Ranked as India's greatest hero in many surveys. Martyrs' Day: March 23.

QuestionText: What is the role of the Supreme Court of India?
Options: A) Makes laws for the nation
B) The apex judicial body — guardian of the Constitution, interprets laws, final court of appeal, protects Fundamental Rights
C) Controls the executive branch of government
D) Only adjudicates disputes between states
Explanation: Supreme Court of India: apex judicial authority. Functions: Guardian of the Constitution (declares laws unconstitutional if they violate Constitution), Appellate jurisdiction (final court of appeal from High Courts), Original jurisdiction (disputes between states/Centre and states), Advisory jurisdiction (President can seek its opinion), Protection of Fundamental Rights (Article 32 — citizens can directly approach SC for FR violations). 34 judges including Chief Justice. Located at Tilak Marg, New Delhi. Current CJI (Chief Justice of India) heads the judiciary. PIL (Public Interest Litigation) allows citizens to approach SC on public interest matters.

QuestionText: What was the Jalliawala Bagh massacre?
Options: A) A naval battle between India and Britain in 1919
B) British forces firing on unarmed civilians at Jalliawala Bagh, Amritsar in 1919 — killing 379+ people
C) A partition-related riot in Punjab in 1947
D) An Indian attack on British soldiers in 1919
Explanation: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre: April 13, 1919 (Baisakhi day). British General Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire on a peaceful gathering of 15,000-20,000 unarmed civilians (protesting Rowlatt Act) in a walled garden in Amritsar, Punjab — without warning. Official count: 379 killed; Indian National Congress estimated 1,000+. Only exit gates were used for firing. Dyer blocked exits deliberately. The massacre shocked India and world — radicalised the independence movement. Rabindranath Tagore returned his knighthood in protest. Britain formally expressed 'regret' but never apologised (2019, 100th anniversary).

QuestionText: What is the Indian Parliament?
Options: A) The President and Council of Ministers
B) India's supreme legislative body comprising the President, Lok Sabha (lower house), and Rajya Sabha (upper house)
C) Only the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
D) The Supreme Court and Parliament combined
Explanation: Indian Parliament: bicameral (two houses). Lok Sabha (House of the People): 543 elected members + 2 Anglo-Indian nominated members (removed by 104th Amendment), directly elected by citizens. Rajya Sabha (Council of States): 245 members — 238 elected by state assemblies, 12 nominated by President. Lok Sabha more powerful (money bills, no-confidence motion). President: part of Parliament, gives assent to bills. Parliament meets in Parliament House, New Delhi. Sessions: Budget (February-May), Monsoon (July-August), Winter (November-December). Parliament can make laws on Union and Concurrent lists.

QuestionText: Who was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and what is his significance?
Options: A) India's first Prime Minister
B) 'Father of the Indian Constitution' — jurist, economist, social reformer who fought against caste discrimination
C) India's first President
D) Founder of the Indian National Congress
Explanation: Dr. Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar (1891-1956): born into the 'Untouchable' Mahar caste, faced severe caste discrimination but earned multiple PhDs (Columbia University, London School of Economics). Chief architect of India's Constitution. First Law Minister of Independent India. Founded political parties (Independent Labour Party, Republican Party of India), newspaper Mooknayak. Fought for Dalit rights, women's rights, reservation in education and government jobs. Converted to Buddhism on October 14, 1956 with 500,000 followers. Received Bharat Ratna (posthumously, 1990). April 14 (his birthday) is observed as Ambedkar Jayanti — a national holiday.

QuestionText: What is 'Federalism' in the Indian context?
Options: A) A system with only state governments
B) Division of powers between the central (Union) government and state governments, with states having autonomy in their jurisdiction
C) A system where all states follow identical laws
D) The power of local governments to make decisions
Explanation: Indian Federalism: India is a 'Union of States' (Article 1) — the Constitution divides powers between Centre and States. Three lists: Union List (97 subjects — only Parliament can legislate: defence, foreign affairs, atomic energy, currency), State List (66 subjects — only states can legislate: police, agriculture, health), Concurrent List (52 subjects — both can legislate: education, forests, criminal law). In conflict, Centre prevails on Concurrent List. India has 'cooperative federalism' — Centre and States work together. But India's federalism is centralised — Centre is stronger (Presidential Rule, Article 356, spending power).

QuestionText: What was the Partition of Bengal in 1905 and its significance?
Options: A) Bengal's division into districts for administrative efficiency
B) Lord Curzon's division of Bengal into Hindu-majority West and Muslim-majority East — triggered Swadeshi Movement and Indian nationalism
C) Bengal's separation from India in 1905
D) The creation of Bangladesh in 1905
Explanation: Partition of Bengal (1905): Lord Curzon (Viceroy) divided Bengal into East Bengal and Assam (Muslim majority) and West Bengal, Bihar, and Odisha (Hindu majority) — officially for administrative efficiency but widely seen as 'divide and rule' strategy. Triggered the Swadeshi Movement (boycott of British goods, promotion of Indian-made goods) — a major milestone in Indian nationalism. Reunited in 1911 after massive protests. This was one of the first mass political movements in India, drawing millions into the freedom struggle. The partition concept was later revived in 1947 (India-Pakistan partition).

QuestionText: What is the Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) in India?
Options: A) Enforceable rights like Fundamental Rights
B) Non-justiciable guidelines for the state in making laws and policies, aimed at achieving socioeconomic justice
C) Guidelines for the President in administering the country
D) Rules for military conduct
Explanation: DPSP (Part IV, Articles 36-51): guidelines for government policy-making inspired by Irish Constitution and Gandhian principles. Cannot be enforced in court (non-justiciable) but are 'fundamental in governance' (Article 37). Aim: socio-economic justice that Fundamental Rights don't provide. Examples: equal pay for equal work, free legal aid, uniform civil code, prohibition of liquor, living wage, cottage industries. Distinction from FR: FR are negative (restrict state), DPSP are positive (direct state action). DPSP vs FR conflict: Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) — Parliament cannot use DPSPs to destroy FR's basic structure.

QuestionText: What was the role of Rani Lakshmibai in India's freedom struggle?
Options: A) She negotiated India's independence peacefully
B) She led troops against the British during the 1857 Revolt, becoming an iconic symbol of resistance — died in battle
C) She was the first woman elected to the Indian Parliament
D) She led the Quit India Movement in 1942
Explanation: Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi (1828-1858): one of the most heroic leaders of the 1857 Revolt (First War of Indian Independence). When British used 'Doctrine of Lapse' to annex Jhansi (because her adopted son wasn't recognised as heir), she refused to surrender — led armed resistance. Fought the British in battle of Gwalior, died fighting aged ~29-30 (June 17/18, 1858). British General Hugh Rose called her 'the most dangerous of all Indian leaders.' She is a national icon of courage and patriotism. 'Khub ladi mardani woh toh Jhansi wali Rani thi' — famous poem.

QuestionText: What is the significance of the 73rd Constitutional Amendment?
Options: A) It abolished untouchability
B) It established Panchayati Raj — giving constitutional status to rural local self-government with reservation for women and SCs/STs
C) It created the Election Commission
D) It added Fundamental Duties to the Constitution
Explanation: 73rd Constitutional Amendment (1992): gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions (rural local government — third tier of governance). Key provisions: Three-tier system (Gram Panchayat, Panchayat Samiti, Zila Parishad), Reservation of 1/3 seats for women (many states now 50%), Reservation for SCs/STs proportional to their population, State Finance Commissions, State Election Commissions for Panchayat elections, 29 subjects (11th Schedule) that can be devolved to Panchayats. 74th Amendment: same for urban local bodies (municipalities). April 24 celebrated as 'Panchayati Raj Divas.'

QuestionText: What was the Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)?
Options: A) India's refusal to join the United Nations
B) Gandhi's mass movement calling on Indians to boycott British institutions, goods, and services to pressure for self-rule
C) A movement against cooperation between Hindus and Muslims
D) Congress's refusal to cooperate with rival political parties
Explanation: Non-Cooperation Movement: launched September 5, 1920 by Gandhi — India's first mass movement involving common people (not just elites). Called for: boycott of British courts, educational institutions, government jobs, elections; surrender of British titles and honours; promotion of Khadi (handspun cloth); civil disobedience. Joined by millions across castes and religions. Gandhi called it off February 1922 after Chauri Chaura incident (mob burned police station, killing 22 policemen) — Gandhi believed movement needed to be non-violent. The movement demonstrated Congress's mass base and established Gandhi as supreme leader.

QuestionText: Who was Subhas Chandra Bose and what was the INA?
Options: A) A British officer who helped India gain independence
B) A radical freedom fighter who formed the Indian National Army (INA) to fight British India using armed struggle with Japan's support
C) The founder of the Muslim League
D) India's first Defence Minister
Explanation: Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose (1897-1945?): elected Congress President twice (1938, 1939) but resigned due to differences with Gandhi. Escaped British house arrest (1941), sought German and Japanese support. Formed Azad Hind Government (1943, Singapore). Revived and led INA (Indian National Army) with 40,000+ soldiers (including POWs and Indian diaspora from Southeast Asia). INA fought in Imphal-Kohima battles (1944). Disappeared/died in air crash (August 18, 1945 — still controversial). 'Jai Hind' (Victory to India) and 'Dilli Chalo' (March to Delhi) are his slogans. January 23 is Netaji's birthday — Parakram Diwas.

QuestionText: What is the role of the Election Commission of India?
Options: A) Makes electoral laws
B) An independent constitutional body that conducts, controls, and supervises all elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President, and Vice-President
C) Decides election disputes
D) Appoints election candidates
Explanation: Election Commission of India (ECI): established January 25, 1950 (National Voters' Day). Constitutional body under Article 324. Chief Election Commissioner (CEC): head of ECI, has security of tenure (removal requires same process as Supreme Court judge). Functions: conducts Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, State Legislature, President, VP elections; enforces Model Code of Conduct; registers political parties; allocates election symbols; announces election schedule; uses Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and VVPAT. The ECI is considered one of the world's most respected election management bodies. India conducts the world's largest elections.

QuestionText: What were the 'Quit India Movement' (1942)?
Options: A) Gandhi asking Congress to quit politics
B) A mass movement demanding immediate British withdrawal from India, with 'Do or Die' as its motto — launched August 8, 1942
C) A movement for Indians to quit British-owned companies
D) A movement against Indians joining the British army in WWII
Explanation: Quit India Movement (August Kranti): launched August 8-9, 1942 at Gowalia Tank Maidan, Mumbai by Gandhi — demanding immediate independence. 'Do or Die' (Karo ya Maro) motto. British arrested Congress leadership within hours. Without leaders, people led decentralised rebellions — cutting telegraph wires, attacking British officials, establishing parallel governments in some areas. Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted Congress flag at Gowalia Tank. Movement suppressed by British with force — 1,000+ killed, 100,000+ arrested. India gained independence 5 years later (1947). This was India's most decisive independence struggle.

QuestionText: What is the CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General) of India?
Options: A) The head of the Income Tax Department
B) A constitutional authority that audits all accounts of the Union and State Governments, ensuring financial accountability
C) The chief financial officer of the RBI
D) The head of all government banks
Explanation: CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General): established by Article 148. Appointed by President, holds office until 65 years, removable only like Supreme Court judge (independent). Functions: audits all Union and State government expenditures against parliamentary/assembly authorisation; submits reports to Parliament/legislatures; audits public sector enterprises; examines efficiency and economy of government spending. CAG reports have exposed major scams (2G spectrum — estimated ₹1.76 lakh crore loss, Coal scam, Commonwealth Games). CAG is critical for Parliament's financial control over executive.

QuestionText: What is 'judicial review' in India?
Options: A) The President reviewing court judgments
B) The power of courts (especially Supreme Court) to examine laws and government actions and strike them down if they violate the Constitution
C) Annual review of judicial appointments
D) Citizens reviewing the performance of judges
Explanation: Judicial Review: the power of the Supreme Court (and High Courts) to examine whether laws passed by Parliament/state legislatures and actions of the executive are consistent with the Constitution. If found unconstitutional — struck down. Landmark cases: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) — established Basic Structure Doctrine (Parliament cannot amend the Constitution's basic structure), Menaka Gandhi (1978) — expanded Article 21 interpretation, Shah Bano (1985) — Muslim divorce rights, Right to Privacy (2017). India's judicial review is more restricted than the US — courts can strike laws for procedural violations (Article 21 'procedure established by law').

QuestionText: What was India's first General Election?
Explanation: India's first General Election: October 1951 – February 1952 — the world's largest democratic exercise at that time. ~176 million voters (many illiterate — symbol-based voting used). Indian National Congress won a majority. Jawaharlal Nehru became Prime Minister. The election demonstrated that universal adult franchise could work in a newly independent, largely illiterate, diverse nation — despite global scepticism. Conducted by ECI's first CEC Sukumar Sen. The 2024 General Election (18th) had ~970 million eligible voters — world's largest electorate. India has never missed a general election since 1952.

QuestionText: What was the Battle of Plassey (1757)?
Options: A) First battle of the 1857 revolt
B) Battle where British East India Company defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah of Bengal — establishing British dominance in India
C) A naval battle between India and Portugal
D) A battle between Mughals and Marathas
Explanation: Battle of Plassey (June 23, 1757): Robert Clive of the British East India Company defeated Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah of Bengal with crucial support of Mir Jafar (betrayal). This victory established the Company's dominance in Bengal and marked the beginning of British political control over India. The Company gained the right to collect revenue in Bengal. This is considered the foundation of British rule in India — transforming the Company from a trading entity to a political power. Mir Jafar (who betrayed the Nawab) became a symbol of treachery — 'Mir Jafar' is still used as a term for a traitor in India.

QuestionText: What is the Fundamental Duties provision in the Indian Constitution?
Options: A) Part of the original 1950 Constitution
B) Added by 42nd Amendment (1976) — 11 duties of citizens including abiding by the Constitution, respecting national flag, promoting harmony
C) Rights that citizens must pay taxes to maintain
D) Obligations of the government towards citizens
Explanation: Fundamental Duties (Article 51A, Part IV-A): added by 42nd Constitutional Amendment (1976) during Emergency, based on Swaran Singh Committee recommendations, inspired by USSR Constitution. Originally 10 duties; 11th added by 86th Amendment (2002) — duty to provide education opportunities to children aged 6-14. Examples: abide by Constitution, cherish Constitution's ideals, defend integrity and sovereignty, protect natural environment, promote scientific temper, safeguard public property, strive for excellence. Non-justiciable (cannot be enforced by courts). All citizens have these duties — not foreigners. They mirror the FR — rights and duties are complementary.

QuestionText: Who designed the Indian national flag?
Options: A) Rabindranath Tagore
B) Pingali Venkayya
C) Mahatma Gandhi
D) Nehru
Explanation: Pingali Venkayya (1876-1963): freedom fighter from Andhra Pradesh who designed the flag of India. Presented designs to Gandhi who selected one and suggested replacing the spinning wheel with the Ashoka Chakra. Official flag (adopted July 22, 1947): three equal horizontal bands — deep saffron (courage, sacrifice), white (peace, truth), India green (fertility, faith), with Ashoka Chakra (24-spoke navy blue wheel from Ashoka's Sarnath Lion Capital — the wheel of law/Dharma Chakra). The flag is made from khadi (handspun cloth) — BIS standards. Flag Code of India: regulates display of the national flag.

QuestionText: What is the significance of the Constituent Assembly?
Options: A) It governed India after independence
B) An elected body (December 1946) that drafted and adopted the Indian Constitution over 2 years 11 months
C) It was the first Parliament of independent India
D) It selected India's first President and PM
Explanation: Constituent Assembly: body of 299 members elected by provincial assemblies (December 1946) to draft India's Constitution. Chaired by Dr. Rajendra Prasad. Drafting Committee chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. Deliberated from December 9, 1946 to November 26, 1949 — 2 years 11 months 18 days. 166 days of active debate. Adopted November 26, 1949 (Constitution Day). Came into effect January 26, 1950. The Assembly drew from constitutions worldwide: UK (Parliamentary system), USA (FR, judicial review, President as executive head), Ireland (DPSP), Canada (Federation), Australia (Concurrent list), South Africa (amendment procedure).

QuestionText: What was the partition of India in 1947?
Options: A) Division of India into North and South zones
B) The division of British India into two independent nations — India (Hindu majority) and Pakistan (Muslim majority) on August 14-15, 1947
C) Division of India into states based on language
D) Separation of Indian provinces from the British Crown
Explanation: Partition of India: British India was divided into India (August 15) and Pakistan (August 14, 1947 — including present-day Bangladesh, then East Pakistan). Mountbatten Plan (June 1947) and Radcliffe Line (drawn by Cyril Radcliffe in 5 weeks). Causes: Congress-Muslim League conflict, Two-Nation Theory (Jinnah — Muslims need a separate nation). Consequences: ~14 million people displaced (one of history's largest migrations), ~200,000-2 million killed in communal violence, lasting India-Pakistan hostility. East Pakistan became Bangladesh in 1971 (after Bangladesh Liberation War). August 14 is now Partition Horrors Remembrance Day in India.

QuestionText: What is the significance of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel?
Options: A) First President of India
B) 'Iron Man of India' — first Deputy PM who integrated 562 princely states into the Indian Union after independence
C) Founder of the Indian National Congress
D) Chief author of the Indian Constitution
Explanation: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (1875-1950): India's first Deputy PM and Home Minister. Known as 'Iron Man of India' for his firm approach to national integration. His greatest achievement: integrating 562 princely states (Hyderabad, Junagadh, Kashmir, Travancore, etc.) into India through diplomacy and, when necessary, force (Police Action in Hyderabad — Operation Polo, September 1948). Without Patel's integration, India might have fragmented into hundreds of kingdoms. Statue of Unity (Gujarat): world's tallest statue (182m) built in his honour (2018). October 31 (his birthday) is Rashtriya Ekta Diwas (National Unity Day).

QuestionText: What are Fundamental Rights? Which right allows citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court?
Options: A) Article 21 — Right to Life
B) Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies — the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' per Dr. Ambedkar
C) Article 19 — Freedom of Speech
D) Article 14 — Right to Equality
Explanation: Article 32 — Right to Constitutional Remedies: allows citizens to directly approach the Supreme Court (and Article 226 allows approaching High Courts) to enforce Fundamental Rights. The SC can issue writs: Habeas Corpus (produce the detained person — protects against illegal detention), Mandamus (order public authority to perform duty), Prohibition (lower court cannot exceed jurisdiction), Certiorari (quash lower court order), Quo Warranto (question authority to hold public office). Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul of the Constitution' because FR without enforcement are meaningless.

QuestionText: What was the 1857 Revolt?
Options: A) A minor mutiny among British troops
B) India's first major uprising against British rule — called the Sepoy Mutiny by British, First War of Independence by Indians
C) A revolution led by educated Indian classes
D) An economic protest against British taxation
Explanation: 1857 Revolt (Sepoy Mutiny / First War of Independence): began May 10, 1857 in Meerut when sepoys refused greased cartridges (rumoured to contain pig and cow fat — offensive to Muslims and Hindus). Spread across north and central India — Delhi, Awadh, Jhansi, Kanpur, Bareilly. Leaders: Bahadur Shah Zafar (last Mughal), Rani Lakshmibai, Nana Sahib, Tatya Tope, Begum Hazrat Mahal. Suppressed by British by 1858. Consequences: British Crown took over from East India Company; India formally became part of British Empire; British Queen became Empress of India (1876). It was the most significant challenge to British rule before Gandhi's movements.

QuestionText: What is the UPSC (Union Public Service Commission)?
Options: A) An education policy making body
B) A constitutional body conducting civil service examinations for recruitment to central government services (IAS, IPS, IFS, etc.)
C) A parliamentary committee on public policy
D) An organisation for university accreditation
Explanation: UPSC (Union Public Service Commission): established under Article 315. Constitutional body conducting: Civil Services Examination (IAS — Indian Administrative Service, IPS — Police, IFS — Foreign Service, etc.), Engineering Services Exam, NDA exam, CDS exam, and many others. Chairman and members appointed by President, cannot be dismissed except by process like Supreme Court judge. Considers applications from approximately 1 million candidates for ~1,000 posts annually — among the most competitive exams globally. Each state has its own PSC (State Public Service Commission) for state civil services (PCS — Provincial Civil Service).

QuestionText: What is the significance of the Emergency period (1975-77) in India?
Options: A) A period when India faced military emergency from China
B) PM Indira Gandhi declared a national emergency (1975-77) — suspending Fundamental Rights, press freedom, and holding elections — ended after defeat in 1977 elections
C) A period of severe economic emergency in India
D) An environmental emergency due to drought and famine
Explanation: Emergency (June 25, 1975 – March 21, 1977): President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed proclaimed national emergency under Article 352 on PM Indira Gandhi's advice — citing 'internal disturbance.' Triggered by: Allahabad High Court ruling Gandhi's 1971 election invalid, JP (Jayaprakash Narayan) Movement. During Emergency: Press censorship (newspapers ran blank editorials), Fundamental Rights suspended (including Habeas Corpus), Opposition leaders arrested (Atal Bihari Vajpayee, L.K. Advani, etc.), forced sterilisation programme (Sanjay Gandhi), 42nd Amendment passed. Gandhi called elections (1977) and lost to Janata Party — Emergency ended. This remains India's most controversial political chapter.

QuestionText: Assertion: India is described as a 'secular' state in the Constitution. Reason: India adopted secularism meaning the state has no official religion and treats all religions equally. Which is correct?
Options: A) Both assertion and reason are true; reason correctly explains assertion
B) Both true but reason does not explain assertion
C) Assertion true; reason false
D) Both false
Explanation: Assertion TRUE: 'Secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Reason TRUE and correctly explains: Indian secularism means: state has no official/established religion, all religions are treated equally by the state, state will not discriminate on grounds of religion, state maintains religious neutrality. Indian secularism differs from French laïcité (strict church-state separation) — India involves itself in all religions equally (rather than complete separation). Constitutional provisions: Articles 25-28 (Freedom of Religion) guarantee religious freedom while ensuring state neutrality.

QuestionText: Who were the British East India Company?
Options: A) A British government organisation
B) A British trading company (est. 1600) that transformed from traders to rulers of India — controlling much of India before the 1857 Revolt
C) A company importing Indian goods to Britain only
D) A British company established in India after independence
Explanation: British East India Company: established December 31, 1600 by Queen Elizabeth I's Royal Charter. Initially a trading company dealing in spices, textiles, indigo. Evolution: Battle of Plassey (1757) gave political dominance in Bengal; gradually expanded. By early 19th century: controlled most of India, maintained its own army (sepoys). Collected taxes, administered law, made treaties. After 1857 Revolt: British Crown abolished the Company (1858) and took direct control — India became part of the British Empire under the India Act 1858. The Company's business practices, including exploitation of Indian weavers and farmers, caused de-industrialisation of India.

QuestionText: What is the role of the Prime Minister in India?
Options: A) Head of State
B) Head of Government — leads Council of Ministers, runs the executive, commands parliamentary majority
C) Head of the Supreme Court
D) Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces
Explanation: Prime Minister (PM): Head of Government in India's parliamentary system. Appointed by President (leader of majority party/coalition in Lok Sabha). Real executive power rests with PM and Council of Ministers. PM: chairs Cabinet meetings, coordinates government policy, advises President on all major decisions, leads in Parliament. President: constitutional/ceremonial Head of State. Council of Ministers responsible to Lok Sabha. PM has a unique constitutional position — can advise President to dissolve Lok Sabha. India's PMs: Nehru (longest — 1947-1964), Modi (current — since 2014, 15th PM serving third term from 2024).

QuestionText: What is the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC)?
Options: A) A court for trying human rights violators
B) A statutory body investigating human rights violations by state and central governments
C) A UN body monitoring India's human rights
D) A committee of Parliament for human rights
Explanation: NHRC (National Human Rights Commission): established under Protection of Human Rights Act 1993. Quasi-judicial body investigating complaints of human rights violations by government/state officials. Chairman: retired Chief Justice of India. Can: examine complaints, visit jails and detention centres, review safeguards for human rights, promote human rights education, recommend compensation to victims. Limitations: cannot investigate defence forces (separate complaints body), complaints must be made within one year, recommendations are not binding (but largely followed). State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs) exist at state level.

QuestionText: What was the role of Jawaharlal Nehru in modern India?
Options: A) Chief architect of India's Constitution
B) India's first Prime Minister — shaped India's foreign policy (Non-Alignment), industrial policy, democratic institutions, and scientific temper
C) Leader of India's independence army
D) Founder of the Indian National Congress
Explanation: Jawaharlal Nehru (1889-1964): India's first PM (1947-1964 — longest serving). Shaped modern India: Non-Aligned Movement (NAM) co-founder — India's independent foreign policy. Planned economy with Five-Year Plans (Mahalanobis model — focus on heavy industry). Established IITs, IIMs, AIIMS, NITs, nuclear programme, ISRO precursor. Promoted scientific temper and secularism. India-China relations deteriorated (1962 war). 'Discovery of India' (book) explained India's cultural history. Children's Day: November 14 (his birthday — Chacha Nehru). His vision of democratic, secular, socialist India shaped the Constitution.

QuestionText: What is Habeas Corpus?
Options: A) A constitutional amendment procedure
B) A writ requiring a detained person to be brought before a court to determine if the detention is lawful — protects against illegal imprisonment
C) A power of the President to pardon convicts
D) A fundamental right to education
Explanation: Habeas Corpus ('you shall have the body'): a writ issued by Supreme Court or High Courts requiring a person detaining another to produce the detained person in court and justify the detention. If detention is unlawful — person must be released. Protects against arbitrary arrest and illegal detention. Suspended during national emergency (controversial during 1975-77 Emergency — ADM Jabalpur case). Significant cases: ADM Jabalpur vs Shivkant Shukla (1976 — controversial SC ruling allowing suspension during Emergency), later overruled by Puttaswamy (2017) judgment emphasising personal liberty. Most powerful remedy for illegal detention.

QuestionText: What were the Simon Commission protests and their significance?
Options: A) Indian soldiers refusing British orders in WWI
B) A movement against the all-British Simon Commission (1927) reviewing India's constitution — no Indian members — triggered 'Go Back Simon' protests and Lala Lajpat Rai's death
C) Protests against British import of Simon goods
D) A workers' strike against the Simon Coal Company
Explanation: Simon Commission: appointed November 1927, chaired by Sir John Simon — 7 British MPs to review the Government of India Act 1919. NO Indian member. Indians were incensed by exclusion from deciding their own constitutional future. 'Go Back Simon' protests across India. Lala Lajpat Rai led protests in Lahore (October 30, 1928) — police lathi charge injured him severely, he died on November 17, 1928. Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, Sukhdev assassinated police officer Saunders in retaliation. The commission's report contributed to the Government of India Act 1935. Commission's exclusion of Indians strengthened the independence movement.

QuestionText: What is India's 'Basic Structure Doctrine'?
Options: A) The basic physical infrastructure the government must provide
B) A judicial doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati case, 1973) that Parliament cannot amend certain fundamental features of the Constitution
C) The basic structure of the Indian Parliament
D) Foundational economic policies that cannot be changed
Explanation: Basic Structure Doctrine: established by Supreme Court in Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala (1973) — 13-judge bench, decided 7:6. Parliament can amend the Constitution (Article 368) but cannot alter its 'basic structure.' Basic structure elements (not exhaustively defined): Supremacy of the Constitution, Democratic and republican form of government, Secularism, Federalism, Separation of powers, Judicial review, Fundamental Rights. This doctrine prevents Parliament from using its amendment power to destroy constitutional democracy. Used in Indira Gandhi vs Raj Narain (1975) and many subsequent cases. Considered one of India's most significant judicial developments.

QuestionText: What was the First Five-Year Plan of India?
Explanation: India's First Five-Year Plan: 1951-1956. Based on Harrod-Domar growth model. Priority: agriculture (food self-sufficiency — inspired by food shortage memories and Bengal famine 1943), irrigation, power generation. Bhakra Nangal Dam: major project. Success: GDP growth exceeded target (3.6% vs 2.1% target). Planning Commission (established 1950) made Five-Year Plans until 12th Plan (2012-17). Nehru called large dams 'temples of modern India.' NITI Aayog replaced Planning Commission in 2015. Second Plan (1956-61): heavy industrialisation (Mahalanobis model) — steel plants, Bhilai (Soviet-aided), Rourkela, Durgapur.

QuestionText: What is the Representation of the People Act in India?
Options: A) Act guaranteeing the right to be represented by a lawyer
B) Legislation governing elections — voter eligibility, election procedures, conduct, disputes, and disqualification of candidates
C) Act giving minorities reserved representation in Parliament
D) Act requiring all government schemes to represent all communities
Explanation: Representation of the People Act, 1950 and 1951: foundational electoral legislation. Covers: qualifications for voting (Indian citizen, 18+ years, registered, not disqualified), delimitation of constituencies, election schedules, nomination process, election expenses limits, disqualification of candidates (criminal convictions, holding office of profit), election disputes (election petitions to High Courts), offences (bribery, booth capture). Supreme Court has used this act to disqualify convicted MPs/MLAs. Electoral Roll (voters' list) maintained under this Act. Model Code of Conduct operates alongside this Act during elections.

QuestionText: Who was Raja Ram Mohan Roy and what was his significance?
Options: A) A Mughal Emperor who patronised Indian arts
B) 19th-century social reformer who fought against sati, child marriage, and caste discrimination — 'Father of Indian Renaissance'
C) A general who fought British in 1857
D) A Congress president in the early 20th century
Explanation: Raja Ram Mohan Roy (1772-1833): Indian social reformer, scholar, and humanist — 'Father of the Indian Renaissance.' Fought against: Sati (widow immolation — got it banned by Governor-General Bentinck in 1829 through Bengal Sati Regulation), child marriage, caste discrimination, polygamy. Founded Brahmo Samaj (1828) — religious reform movement emphasising monotheism and rational thinking. Advocated for women's education, English education, freedom of press, and Western scientific learning. Met British intellectuals and politicians in England. Died in Bristol, UK (1833). Set foundation for India's modernisation and reform movements.

QuestionText: What is the significance of the Indian National Congress (INC) founding?
Options: A) It was founded to help the British govern India
B) India's oldest political party (founded 1885) that led the independence movement — dominant party for 40+ years post-independence
C) It was India's first government after independence
D) It was founded by Mahatma Gandhi
Explanation: Indian National Congress (INC): founded December 28, 1885 by Allan Octavian Hume (a British civil servant) in Bombay. First session chaired by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee. Initially moderate — petitioned British for reforms. Became radical post-1905 partition of Bengal. Mass movement under Gandhi (1920s-1940s). Post-independence: dominant party — Nehru (17 years), Indira Gandhi, Rajiv Gandhi as PMs. Lost power 1977 (Emergency backlash), returned 1980. INC leads UPA coalition. 2014 and 2019 and 2024: INC lost general elections to BJP. INC remains the largest opposition party. Party symbol: hand.

QuestionText: What is the Rajya Sabha and how are its members selected?
Options: A) Directly elected by all voters
B) The upper house of Parliament — members elected by elected MLAs of state legislatures + 12 members nominated by President for expertise
C) Appointed by the Prime Minister from distinguished citizens
D) Members are senior Lok Sabha members automatically elevated
Explanation: Rajya Sabha (Council of States): upper house of India's bicameral Parliament. 245 members: 233 elected by state/UT legislative assemblies using single transferable vote, 12 nominated by President (for expertise in literature, science, art, social service). Permanent body — never dissolved (unlike Lok Sabha). 1/3 of members retire every 2 years. Term: 6 years. Chairman: Vice-President of India (ex officio). Current Chairman: Jagdeep Dhankhar. Powers: equal to Lok Sabha on ordinary bills, constitutional amendments; cannot vote on Money Bills (Lok Sabha's prerogative). Rajya Sabha represents the states in Parliament — federal principle.

QuestionText: What is the 'Right to Information' (RTI) Act?
Options: A) Right to receive news broadcasts freely
B) A law giving citizens the right to request information from government departments — promoting transparency and accountability
C) Right to access internet
D) Right to information about criminal history of politicians
Explanation: RTI Act 2005: landmark transparency legislation. Any citizen can file an RTI application to any government body requesting information — must respond within 30 days (48 hours for life/liberty matters). Central Information Commission (CIC) and State Information Commissions (SICs) handle appeals. Has exposed: corruption in MGNREGA, exam paper leaks, government inaction, unexplained public spending. Exemptions: national security, cabinet papers, third-party commercial information, parliamentary privilege. First Information Commissioner: Wajahat Habibullah. RTI is a powerful anti-corruption tool — millions of applications filed annually. Activists have used it effectively to demand government accountability.

QuestionText: What was the Maurya Empire's significance in ancient Indian history?
Options: A) India's first democracy
B) India's first large unified empire (321-185 BCE) under Chandragupta Maurya and Emperor Ashoka — spread Buddhism globally
C) The empire that built the Taj Mahal
D) The empire that resisted Mughal invasion
Explanation: Maurya Empire (321-185 BCE): India's first great empire, founded by Chandragupta Maurya (advised by Kautilya/Chanakya). Extended from Afghanistan to Bengal, from Himalayas to Deccan. Ashoka the Great (269-232 BCE): after the bloody Kalinga War (~261 BCE) he embraced Buddhism and non-violence (Ahimsa). Spread Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Greece, Egypt, West Asia through rock edicts and pillars (Ashoka Chakra from Sarnath pillar is on India's flag). Arthashastra (Kautilya): early treatise on statecraft and economic policy. The Mauryan empire laid foundations for the concept of pan-Indian unity.
